corrected_value.title: Association of estrogen receptor gene polymorphisms with susceptibility to adolescent idiopathic scoliosis

decisions.location: Background and Purpose, lines 4-6; see also Methods, Results, Conclusions and discussion, and References, lines 8-12
decisions.quote:
It has been suggested that XbaI single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) (A/G rs934099) in estrogen receptor 1 (ESR1) may be associated with curve severity in Japanese AIS patients[ 1 ] and with both curve severity and predisposition for AIS in Chinese patients[ 2 ]. However, replication studies have not confirmed these findings[ 3 ]. The role of the XbaI ESR1 polymorphism rs9340799 in AIS has never been described in Caucasian AIS patients. 
 Purpose 
 A genetic association study was performed to investigate the association between XbaI SNP in ESR1 and the predisposition for, or progression of, AIS in Caucasian patients.
decisions.reason: Janusz et al. (2013, 10.1186/1748-7161-8-s2-o2) explicitly re-test both previously reported ESR1 XbaI (rs9340799) associations in a Caucasian sample of 286 female AIS patients and 116 healthy female controls: (1) association with curve severity/progression/operation rate first reported in Japanese AIS patients by Inoue et al. (2002, 10.1097/00007632-200211010-00009, shipped row 2495, target_index 0), and (2) association with both predisposition (case-control susceptibility) for AIS and curve severity reported in Chinese AIS patients by Wu et al. (2006, Spine 31(10):1131-1136, 10.1097/01.brs.0000216603.91330.6f, candidate target_index 1). Janusz et al. empirically test case-control allele/genotype frequencies (predisposition/susceptibility: p=0.63 and p=0.35) as well as progression velocity, mean Cobb angle, and surgery rate, concluding that 'No association between ESR1 XbaI polymorphism and AIS was found in the Caucasian population. None of the previously reported associations with curve severity, progression or operation rate could be confirmed.' Wu et al. (2006) is an independent primary study by a distinct research group in a distinct cohort testing the susceptibility claim directly evaluated here, and it is absent from the shipped rows (which contain only Inoue et al. 2002, row 2495). Both listed prior adjudication/state files (b7f058b4...json and 5626af31...json) are absent.
